title: Cascode Stage
intro: A cascode stacks a common-gate device on a common-source device: the CS device turns the input voltage into a current and the CG device passes it to the output. The result is an output resistance about $g_m r_o$ times higher (Razavi, Section 3.6).

blocks.alt: Schematic of a cascode amplifier. Two NMOS transistors are stacked: M1 at the bottom has its source grounded and its gate driven by Vin; M2 above it has its gate held at a bias voltage Vb. The drain of M2 connects to the supply VDD through the resistor RD, and the output Vout is taken there. The node between the two transistors is marked X.
blocks.caption: A (telescopic) cascode. M1 is the input device, M2 the cascode device; M2 holds node X nearly still.

blocks.text: How it behaves

items: Input change: M1's current changes by $g_{m1}\Delta V$. That current flows into the source of M2, where it sees about $1/g_{m2}$, so X moves by only $(g_{m1}/g_{m2})\Delta V$; the full current reaches $R_D$, giving the same output change as a plain CS stage.
Change of the cascode bias $V_b$ (with $r_{o1} = \infty$): M2 acts as a follower to X, so X moves by the same amount, but the current is fixed by M1, so the output does not move.
With $\lambda = 0$ the gain is exactly the CS gain $-g_{m1}R_D$, regardless of M2's $g_m$ or body effect, because all of M1's signal current goes through M2.

blocks.text: Bias and headroom

M2 sets $V_X = V_b - V_{GS2}$. M1 needs $V_X \ge V_{in} - V_{TH1}$, so $V_b \ge V_{in} - V_{TH1} + V_{GS2}$; M2 needs $V_{out} \ge V_b - V_{TH2}$. With $V_b$ chosen to put M1 at the edge of saturation, the lowest output is

Stacking M2 costs at least one more overdrive of swing (loosely, two $V_{D,sat}$). Sweeping $V_{in}$ upward: both devices are off and $V_X \approx V_b - V_{TH2}$; then current flows, $V_{out}$ falls and $V_X$ falls as $V_{GS2}$ grows; finally either M1 enters triode ($V_X$ below $V_{in} - V_{TH1}$) or M2 does ($V_{out}$ below $V_b - V_{TH2}$), whichever comes first depending on $V_b$ and sizes. Deep in M2's triode region $V_X$ and $V_{out}$ become almost equal.
Output resistance and gain
Seen from the output, the cascode is M2 degenerated by $r_{o1}$:

With an ideal current-source load, $G_m \approx g_{m1}$ and the gain approaches the square of the intrinsic gain, $(g_{m2} + g_{mb2})r_{o2}\,g_{m1}r_{o1}$. Exactly, a little of M1's current is lost in $r_{o1}$ (the source of M2 is $\frac{1}{g_{m2} + g_{mb2}} \parallel r_{o2}$, not zero), giving
A triple cascode raises $R_{out}$ again, but the minimum output voltage becomes three overdrives, so it is rarely worth it.
Cascode or a longer device?

Quadrupling $L$ of a CS device at the same $W$ and current doubles its overdrive, so it uses the same headroom as a cascode. But since $g_m r_o \propto \sqrt{W L/I_D}$, it only doubles $g_m r_o$ (and halves $g_m$), while the cascode multiplies $R_{out}$ by about $g_m r_o$. For a given headroom, cascoding wins.
Cascode current sources and loads
A cascode also makes a better current source. Making the load of an NMOS cascode a PMOS cascode gives an amplifier whose output resistance is two cascode resistances in parallel:

blocks.alt: Four transistors stacked between VDD and ground. From the top: PMOS M4 with gate at Vb3, PMOS M3 with gate at Vb2, the output node Vout, NMOS M2 with gate at Vb1, and NMOS M1 with gate driven by Vin and source at ground. The upper pair is labelled cascode current source and the lower pair cascode amplifier.
blocks.caption: NMOS cascode amplifier with a PMOS cascode load.

blocks.text: Choosing each bias to put M1 and M4 at the edge of saturation, the output can swing from $V_{ov1} + V_{ov2}$ up to $V_{DD} - |V_{ov3}| - |V_{ov4}|$: $V_{DD}$ minus four overdrives. As with any two high-impedance sources in series, the DC output level is not defined by the circuit itself, so it must be set by a feedback loop.
Poor man's cascode

Stacking two devices with their gates tied together (no separate cascode bias) does not give a cascode if both have the same threshold. The bottom device's drain-source voltage is then $V_{GS,bot} - V_{GS,top}$, which is less than its own overdrive, so it sits in triode, and two identical devices behave like one device of twice the length. It works when the top (cascode) device has the lower threshold: the bottom device is saturated if $V_{TH,bot} - V_{TH,top} \ge V_{ov,top}$, for example a 150 mV threshold difference with under 100 mV of overdrive.
Shielding

The high output resistance means a change $\Delta V$ at the output reaches the source of the cascode device attenuated by about $(g_m + g_{mb})r_o$. The cascode device shields the input device from the output. Example: two identical current sources whose drains sit $\Delta V$ apart differ in current by about $I_D\lambda\Delta V$; with cascode devices added, the drain difference of the lower devices is only $\Delta V/[(g_{m3} + g_{mb3})r_{o3}]$, so the mismatch shrinks by that factor.

Shielding fails if the cascode device enters triode: as the output falls below $V_{b2} - V_{TH2}$, M2 needs more overdrive to carry the current, so its source must fall with the output, and eventually M1 is pushed into triode too. A side benefit in nanometer processes: in a cascode no single device has to withstand the full supply, which helps stay inside stress limits when $V_{DD}$ is high.

widget.title: Why cascoding matters: output current of a basic vs cascode mirror

blocks.text: The cascode mirror (flat line) plays the same role as the cascode stage: much higher output resistance, so the current barely changes with $V_{out}$, but only above about $V_{TH} + 2V_{ov}$, which is the headroom cost.
The input and cascode devices need not be the same type: see Folded Cascode.

blocks.title: Cascode output resistance
blocks.text: $g_{m1} = g_{m2} = 1\text{ mS}$, $r_{o1} = r_{o2} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$, no body effect. Find $R_{out}$ and compare with a single device.

blocks.title: Cascode headroom
blocks.text: $V_{ov1} = V_{ov2} = 0.2\text{ V}$ and $V_{TH} = 0.5\text{ V}$. Find the gate bias of M2 that maximizes swing and the minimum output voltage.
solution: M1 needs $V_{DS1} \ge 0.2\text{ V}$, so X should sit at 0.2 V. $V_{GS2} = 0.7\text{ V}$, so $V_{b} = 0.9\text{ V}$.
M2 needs $V_{DS2} \ge 0.2\text{ V}$: $V_{out,min} = 0.4\text{ V}$. A higher $V_b$ only raises X and wastes swing.

blocks.title: Swing and gain of a full cascode
blocks.text: In the four-transistor cascode amplifier, $V_{DD} = 1.8\text{ V}$, the NMOS overdrives are 0.15 V and the PMOS overdrives 0.2 V. $g_{m1} = g_{m2} = 1\text{ mS}$ with $r_{o1} = r_{o2} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$; $g_{m3} = 1\text{ mS}$ with $r_{o3} = r_{o4} = 25\text{ k}\Omega$. Find the output swing and the approximate gain.
solution: NMOS side: $g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1} = 2.5\text{ M}\Omega$; PMOS side: $g_{m3}r_{o3}r_{o4} = 0.625\text{ M}\Omega$; in parallel $0.5\text{ M}\Omega$. $|A_v| \approx 1\text{ mS} \cdot 0.5\text{ M}\Omega = 500$.

blocks.title: Shielding against mismatch
blocks.text: Two current sources of $100\,\mu\text{A}$ with $\lambda = 0.1\text{ V}^{-1}$ have drains 0.5 V apart. Estimate their current difference, then the difference after adding cascode devices with $(g_m + g_{mb})r_o = 40$.
solution: Without cascodes: $\Delta I \approx I_D\lambda\Delta V = 100\,\mu\text{A} \cdot 0.05 = 5\,\mu\text{A}$ (5 percent).
With cascodes the lower drains differ by only $0.5/40 = 12.5\text{ mV}$, so $\Delta I \approx 0.125\,\mu\text{A}$.

blocks.title: Poor man's cascode
blocks.text: Two stacked NMOS devices share a gate. The top one has $V_{TH} = 0.3\text{ V}$ and the bottom one $V_{TH} = 0.45\text{ V}$; both run at 0.08 V overdrive. Is the bottom device saturated?
solution: The middle node sits $V_{GS,top} = 0.38\text{ V}$ below the shared gate, and the bottom device's source is $V_{GS,bot} = 0.53\text{ V}$ below it, so $V_{DS,bot} = 0.53 - 0.38 = 0.15\text{ V}$.
That exceeds its overdrive of 0.08 V, so it is saturated with 70 mV to spare. With equal thresholds $V_{DS,bot}$ would equal the overdrive difference, zero here: triode.
blocks.answer: Yes: its drain-source voltage (0.15 V) exceeds its 0.08 V overdrive.
